title: Actualization, Records, and the Emergence of Entropic Time
abstract: We develop a record-based account of internal time in quantum mechanics, where the formation of a stable record is represented as conditioning on actualized information, and along a history the accumulated record algebras are ordered by inclusion. If the duration of a realized outcome depends only on its conditional Born probability, composes additively under sequential conditioning, and is continuous and calibrated, then the actualization of each outcome contributes an internal duration equal to its surprisal, the negative logarithm of that probability, so that a certain outcome contributes no duration, whereas less likely outcomes contribute larger increments. The ensemble mean of the accumulated clock is the Shannon entropy of the record process, its moment-generating function is fixed by the Rényi entropy spectrum, and the realized clock admits a Doob decomposition into a predictable entropic compensator and a martingale of clock fluctuations, so that each increment is the information gain of the corresponding actualization. Records are characterized by graded criteria of distinguishability, decoherence, and stability. We also clarify the multiple-clock problem: in one fixed context, additivity of two surprisal clocks is equivalent to factorization of the Born distribution in that context, whereas for a pure bipartite state, additivity in every pair of local contexts is equivalent to rank-one factorization of the joint state and to the vanishing of all its $2\times2$ minors.
summary: This paper proposes that internal time in quantum mechanics arises from the accumulation of 'records' formed during actualization events. The duration assigned to an outcome is quantified by its surprisal ($-\ln p$), leading to a pathwise clock whose average value corresponds to the Shannon entropy. It offers a rigorous, information-theoretic foundation for understanding time without external parameters.
main_problem: The paper develops a record-based account of internal time in quantum mechanics, aiming to define temporal order and duration without relying on external time parameters.
main_result: Internal time is identified with the accumulated surprisal ($-\ln p$) associated with actualized outcomes, leading to an ensemble mean clock proportional to the Shannon entropy of the process.
method: The framework uses conditioning on 'records' (actualized information) and derives the temporal measure by imposing consistency requirements on how duration composes additively under sequential quantum measurements.
model_or_system: The model involves quantum states undergoing sequential measurement contexts, where physical history is represented by an accumulating, nested set of stable records ($\Sigma_n$).
key_observables: Surprisal ($-\ln p$), Shannon Entropy ($H$), Rényi entropy spectrum, and the pathwise clock $	au(h_n)$.
important_parameters: The constant $\sigma$ (scaling factor between information gain and time units) and the distinguishability threshold $\epsilon$.
main_assumptions: Key assumptions include that duration depends only on conditional Born probability, that records persist to form a nested history, and that actualization is equivalent to conditioning on this record.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by defining stable records, deriving the pathwise clock proportional to surprisal, establishing the ensemble mean via Shannon entropy, and concluding with mathematical characterizations like Doob decomposition and additivity conditions for multiple clocks.
why_interesting: It provides a deep theoretical link between fundamental information theory (entropy/surprisal) and the emergence of time in quantum mechanics, which is highly relevant to foundational studies in open systems and gravity.
